SEC23A-01.explanation: Because the sentence opens with "Rarely during a dry summer in the orchard's upper terraces," the auxiliary comes before its subject, "its youngest and least established grafted saplings." The head of that subject is "saplings," which is plural; the singular "summer" in the fronted phrase and the shared "its" (which refers to the orchard) do not set the number. The participle "grown" later in the sentence requires the perfect auxiliary "have"; "do" could combine only with the base form "grow." "has its" uses the right auxiliary but is singular, "do its" cannot combine with "grown," and "does its" fails on both counts.

SEC23A-02.explanation: The subject of the verb is "coat"; "of some seeds" only modifies it, so the verb must be the singular "shields." The pronoun names the owner of "tiny embryos," and the embryos belong to the seeds, not to the coat, so the plural "their," referring to "some seeds," is needed. "shield their" makes the verb agree with the nearby "seeds" instead of "coat." "shields its" has the right verb but a pronoun that could only point to the coat, which has no embryos of its own, and "shield its" is wrong on both counts.

SEC23A-03.explanation: The subject is "many a newly trained physician." Although "many" suggests a plural, "many a" is always followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb. The tense is set inside the same sentence by the conditional clause "if the rash appears," whose present-tense verb requires a present-tense main verb. "are" treats "many" as plural, "was" is singular but past and clashes with "appears," and "were" is both plural and past.

SEC23A-04.explanation: The subject is "the premature twins," which is plural. The phrase between the commas, "a single sensor taped to the chest of the smaller infant," is an absolute phrase with its own noun; neither "sensor" nor "infant" is the subject of the verb. The tense is set in the same sentence by "while the nurses review," a present-tense verb, so the main verb must also be present. "is breathing" agrees with "infant" instead of "twins," "were breathing" is plural but past and clashes with "review," and "was breathing" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC23A-05.explanation: The subject is "more swabs," which is plural; "than a single laboratory can screen" is the comparison, and "laboratory" is not the subject of the main verb. The tense is set later in the same sentence by "when the fungus appeared," a past-tense verb, so the main verb must be past; the present "can screen" belongs to the comparison and does not fix the main verb's tense. "was shipped" agrees with "laboratory," "are shipped" is plural but present and clashes with "appeared," and "is shipped" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC23A-06.explanation: The subject is "biochar," which is singular. The words between the commas, "or the charred fragments of crop stalks heated in a sealed kiln," are a gloss that renames biochar; "or" here does not join two alternative subjects, so the plural "fragments" does not make the verb plural. The tense is set in the same sentence by "until the autumn rains return," whose present-tense verb requires a present main verb. "are being spread" agrees with "fragments," "was being spread" is singular but past and clashes with "return," and "were being spread" is wrong in both number and tense.

SEC23A-07.explanation: "Shepherds keep pregnant ewes in a heated barn during the lambing season" is an independent clause, and "newborn lambs left in a cold field can lose dangerous amounts of body heat" is a second one; "for" here means "because" and joins them as a coordinating conjunction, which takes a comma before it. With no mark, "for newborn lambs" reads as a prepositional phrase attached to "season," and the sentence then runs into the verb "can lose" with no proper link. A semicolon or a colon placed before a coordinating conjunction is not the conventional way to join two clauses like these: "season; for" and "season: for" put a clause-ending mark in front of the word that already does the joining.

SEC23A-08.explanation: The correlative "both ... and" pairs two prepositional phrases: "in the grassy strips that bordered the wheat" and "in the hedgerows along the farm lane." Even though the first phrase is long, because it contains the restrictive clause "that bordered the wheat," no punctuation separates the two halves of the pair. "wheat, and in" puts a comma between the paired elements; "wheat; and in" uses a semicolon, which must join independent clauses, but what follows is only a phrase; "wheat and, in" places a comma between "and" and the phrase it introduces.

SEC23B-01.explanation: The verb comes before its subject here: what was "Of greater concern" is "the thin, steeply tilted, and partly weathered seams of clay," whose head noun "seams" is plural, so the singular "concern" at the front of the sentence does not set the verb's number. The clause "when the first rock cores came up" places the whole sentence in the past, so the verb must be past: "were the." "are the" is plural but present, which clashes with "came up." "was the" is past but singular, agreeing with "concern" rather than "seams," and "is the" is both singular and present.

SEC23B-02.explanation: The subject is "All that survives," in which "all" means "everything"; the singular verb "survives" inside it shows that it is singular, so the plural "instruments" beside the blank does not set the number. The clause "when the hilltop observatory closed its doors" names a definite moment in the past, and a verb tied to such a moment must be simple past rather than present perfect: "was packed." "has been packed" is singular but present perfect, which cannot be pinned to the moment named by "closed." "were packed" is past but plural, agreeing with "instruments," and "have been packed" is both plural and present perfect.

SEC23B-03.explanation: "The former" refers to the first of the two things named in the previous sentence, "a single cup anemometer," not to the "two tipping-bucket rain gauges," so it is singular; the plural "pines" at the end of the interrupting phrase "bolted to a steel mast high above the surrounding pines" is not the subject. The clause "whenever a storm brings gusts" describes a repeated present event, so the main verb must be present as well: "is checked." "are checked" is present but plural, agreeing with "pines" or with the gauges. "was checked" is singular but past, which clashes with "brings," and "were checked" is both plural and past.

SEC23B-04.explanation: The subject is "The walkers' footsteps," which is plural; "not the steady breeze" is set off by commas and only denies a second possible cause, so the singular "breeze" beside the blank does not control the verb. The clause "as hundreds of people crossed" places the action in the past, so the verb must be past progressive: "were shaking." "are shaking" is plural but present, which clashes with "crossed." "was shaking" is past but singular, agreeing with "breeze," and "is shaking" is both singular and present.

SEC23B-05.explanation: The subject of the relative clause is "the longest of which," meaning the longest single tunnel, so it is singular even though "which" stands for the plural "tunnels." The clause "until groundwater broke through a weak joint" places the lining work in the past, so the verb must be past: "was being lined." "is being lined" is singular but present, which clashes with "broke." "were being lined" is past but plural, agreeing with "tunnels," and "are being lined" is both plural and present.

SEC23B-06.explanation: The than-clause has its own subject, "the coarse, stony terraces on the lower slopes," whose head noun "terraces" is plural; the singular "loess" is the subject of the main clause, not of this one. The verb at the end of the than-clause stands in for the main clause's verb "holds," a lexical verb, so the substitute must be a form of "do," and the plural form is "do." "does" is the right kind of verb but singular, copying "loess holds." "are" is plural but a form of "be," which cannot stand in for "holds," and "is" is both singular and a form of "be."

SEC23B-07.explanation: The words before the blank form an independent clause ending in "six refractory clays," and "most broke apart within seconds" is a second independent clause in which "most" is the subject of "broke." Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon between them: "clays; most." "clays, most" joins the clauses with only a comma, a comma splice; read as a phrase renaming "clays," it leaves "broke" without a subject. "clays most" runs the two clauses together with no mark at all. "clays, most," sets "most" off as an aside and again leaves "broke" with no subject.

SEC23B-08.explanation: The words before the blank are a complete clause whose object is itself a finished series, "fine dust, glassy beads formed by meteorite impacts, and three common minerals"; the words after the blank, "plagioclase, pyroxene, and olivine," name those three minerals. A colon after a complete clause can introduce such a list: "minerals: plagioclase." "minerals, plagioclase" merges the two lists into one series that contains "and" twice, so the minerals read as three more items rather than as the three just mentioned. "minerals; plagioclase" leaves a fragment after the semicolon, which must join two independent clauses. "minerals plagioclase" runs the list straight into the noun with no mark.

SEC23C-01.explanation: The subject of the inverted clause comes after the blank: it is "slang" ("new and largely untraceable schoolyard slang"), a singular noun, while "schools" and "leagues" sit inside the fronted phrase "So quickly through secondary schools and their weekend sports leagues" and cannot be the subject, so the auxiliary must be singular. The auxiliary must also be a form of "be": the verb that completes it, "spreading," is an -ing form, which combines with "is" ("is ... spreading"), whereas "does" would need the base form "spread." Only "is new" is both singular and a form of "be." "are new" has the right auxiliary but is plural, agreeing with "leagues." "does new" is singular but cannot combine with "spreading," and "do new" is both plural and the wrong auxiliary.

SEC23C-02.explanation: The relative pronoun "which" refers to the whole compound "both the painted altarpiece and the carved choir screen," two works, so the verb must be plural; "screen," the singular noun just before the comma, is only the second of the two, and the works are restored "side by side," which one object alone cannot be. The verb must also be present, because the restoration happens at the same time as the present-tense "compare" in the while-clause ("while conservators ... compare their pigments"). Only "are being restored" is plural and present. "is being restored" is present but singular, as if "which" referred to "screen" alone. "were being restored" is plural but past, which clashes with "compare" even though the museum "acquired" the works in the past, and "was being restored" is both singular and past.

SEC23C-03.explanation: The subject of the main clause is "hypothesis"; "that the book's two scribes were trained in a single convent workshop" is a clause stating what the hypothesis claims, and its own subject "scribes" (with its plural verb "were trained") is not the subject of the blank, so the verb must be the singular "owes." The pronoun must also refer to "hypothesis," because only a hypothesis can have plausibility owed to evidence; the scribes do not, so the pronoun is the singular "its." Only "owes its" is right on both counts. "owes their" has the right verb but a plural pronoun that would point to "scribes." "owe its" has the right pronoun but a plural verb agreeing with "scribes," and "owe their" makes both errors.

SEC23C-04.explanation: "The founder and first director of the county place-name survey" names a single person, as the single determiner "The" and the later "she" and "her fieldwork" show, so the subject is singular despite "and" and the verb must be singular. The verb must also be past, because the compiling was under way at the moment named by the past-tense when-clause "when she suffered the illness that ended her fieldwork." Only "was compiling" is singular and past. "were compiling" is past but plural, treating the founder and the director as two people. "is compiling" is singular but present, which cannot describe an activity in progress when a past illness ended it, and "are compiling" is both plural and present.

SEC23C-05.explanation: The blank is the verb of the concessive clause "Faded as the frescoes in the two side chapels ______," whose subject is "frescoes," a plural noun; "subject," the singular noun that follows the comma, belongs to the main clause, so the verb must be plural. The verb must also be present: the concession describes the frescoes' condition at the same time as the main clause's present-tense "is easy to identify," and the fading is set against that present ease. Only "are" is plural and present. "is" is present but singular, as if "subject" were its subject. "were" is plural but places the fading in a past that the present-tense main clause does not share, and "was" is both singular and past.

SEC23C-06.explanation: "This last ledger" is the object of the verb, moved to the front of the sentence; the subject is "the two archivists," a plural, so the verb must be plural even though the sentence opens with a singular noun. The verb must also be the past progressive, not the present perfect progressive, because the transcribing was interrupted at a definite past moment, "when a burst pipe flooded the reading room," and the present perfect cannot be tied to a definite past time. Only "were transcribing" is plural and past progressive. "have been transcribing" is plural but present perfect, which clashes with "when a burst pipe flooded." "was transcribing" is past but singular, agreeing with "ledger," and "has been transcribing" is both singular and present perfect.

SEC23C-07.explanation: The subject is "One troupe's surviving props," its verb is "are kept," and between them sits an appositive list naming the props, "a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon," which already contains commas. Because the list has internal commas, it must be set off by two matching dashes, as in "props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon—are." The comma pair in "props, a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are" makes the props read as a fourth item in one long list and then puts a comma between that subject and its verb. "props—a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon, are" opens with a dash but closes with a comma, so the interruption is never properly closed. "props a painted crown, two wooden swords, and a paper moon are" runs the noun "props" straight into the list with nothing to show that the list renames it.

SEC23C-08.explanation: The name "Vidal" identifies which of the three engravers is meant, so it is a restrictive appositive and takes no commas: "only the engraver Vidal signed his plates." The comma pair in "engraver, Vidal," would make the name extra information about a single, already identified engraver, but the passage has just said there were three, so "the engraver" alone does not pick one out. "engraver Vidal," puts a comma between the subject "the engraver Vidal" and its verb "signed." "engraver, Vidal" opens a nonrestrictive interruption with a comma and never closes it.
